newsitem.title: INDIA: Asian wheat demand could pressure world supplies.
newsitem.headline: Asian wheat demand could pressure world supplies.

text.p: Surging Asian and Middle East demand for wheat is likely to put pressure on global supplies but tapping production potential in Ukraine, Kazakhstan and South America could ease the situation, experts said on Wednesday.
"Rising Asian demand will certainly put pressure on the world's wheat supplies," S. Nagarajan, project director in the Directorate of Wheat Research, told Reuters.
Nagarajan said current global trade in wheat was about 105 million tonnes annually out of the world production of about 550 million.
"Wheat trade is growing by about five to seven million tonnes every year due to fast income and population growth," he said.

Timothy Reeves, director general of the Mexico-based International Maize and Wheat Research Centre (CIMMYT), said global wheat demand was expected to double in the next two decades but the area under the crop would remain the same or be reduced.

"Therefore, the only solution lies in doubling the productivity of wheat in all wheat producing nations and meet the rising demand," Reeves said. "This is possible only through better research and policy initiatives by the respective government."
Reeves said there was potential in countries such as Ukraine, Kazakhstan and some South American nations to increase output by increasing the area under the crop.
"I see a significant increase in production from them," Reeves said. "They have the potential to supply to the world market."

He said global prices of wheat were expected to rise in the coming years as world trade in the commodity rose. "As world trade opens up and goes on increasing, prices would increase due to rising global demand."
Reeves said wheat consumption in non-wheat growing countries like Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand was growing at 10 to 15 percent annually.
"The demand from the Middle East countries is also increasing as they still have to import in excess of their own requirement to meet the rising need," Reeves said.
"I also see a large increase in demand from Egypt, Morocco and Libya."
Indian government officials said Australia, the U.S. and Argentina were the only countries which currently had the capacity to export wheat after meeting domestic needs.
"These are the countries which have the funds and also the technology to undertake the research and substantially increase yields to meet the growing export requirement," Nagarajan said.
"Their domestic demand is low as their population is less compared to that of Asian countries."

Reeves said yellow rust disease was currently threatening the wheat crop throughout the world. Investment in better pest control methods and new output-increasing technologies was needed to gradually raise production.
"The yellow rust when it affects the crop reduces output by about 20 percent," Reeves said. "It has significantly affected crops in Pakistan and Iran. We need to find ways to tackle it."
The north Indian town of Karnal is hosting a three-day seminar on wheat research this week.
